# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is an established therapy for the prevention of sudden cardiac death in patients at risk of malignant ventricular arrhythmias [1]. For decades, the conventional transvenous ICD (TV-ICD) was the standard of care, but these systems carry a recognised burden of complications related to their intravascular leads, including infection, pneumothorax, cardiac perforation, venous occlusion, tricuspid dysfunction, and lead fracture or insulation failure [2,3]. Complications associated with transvenous leads are expected to occur after longer follow-up. The subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was developed to provide defibrillation while avoiding these lead-related problems entirely.

## Concept and Early Clinical Experience

The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator was developed to overcome the risk of lead-related complications associated with the transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator; in contrast to the TV-ICD, the S-ICD is a completely extrathoracic device. The feasibility of an entirely extravascular system was first established by Bardy and colleagues, who designed and tested a device requiring no venous access [4]. In their pilot work, ICDs prevent sudden death from cardiac causes in selected patients but require the use of transvenous lead systems, and to eliminate the need for venous access, they designed and tested an entirely subcutaneous ICD system. Single-centre experience subsequently confirmed the clinical applicability of this novel system [5].

Larger early datasets reinforced these findings. In a pooled analysis of the IDE study and EFFORTLESS registry, Burke and colleagues demonstrated effective arrhythmia conversion with acceptable safety [6]. The EFFORTLESS registry, a real-world multicentre cohort, reported favourable short- and long-term outcomes; complication-free rates were 97 and 94%, at 30 and 360 days, respectively. Long-term follow-up of this registry showed that in this diverse S-ICD registry population, spontaneous shock efficacy was consistently high over 5 years, and very few patients underwent S-ICD replacement with a transvenous device for pacing indications [7,8].

## Pivotal Randomised and Observational Evidence

The pivotal randomised comparison came from the PRAETORIAN trial. The PRAETORIAN trial randomized patients with a class I or IIa indication for ICD therapy without the need for pacing to either S-ICD or TV-ICD among 39 centers in the United States and Europe. The trial concluded that in patients with an indication for an ICD but no indication for pacing, the subcutaneous ICD was noninferior to the transvenous ICD with respect to device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [9]. Extended follow-up in PRAETORIAN-XL is examining whether the S-ICD becomes superior at eight years as transvenous lead complications accrue [10].

The UNTOUCHED study addressed a more typical, higher-risk population [11]. Primary prevention patients with left ventricular ejection fraction ≤35% and no pacing indications were included, with generation 2 or 3 S-ICD devices programmed with rate-based therapy and morphology discrimination. Despite this sicker cohort, the study demonstrated high efficacy and safety with contemporary S-ICD devices and programming, and the inappropriate shock rate was the lowest reported for the S-ICD. A post-approval study further confirmed that over a 5-year follow-up, complication rates were low and first and final shock efficacy rates were high [12].

The ATLAS trial randomised younger and higher-risk patients [13]. It found a statistically significant reduction in perioperative, lead-related complications, which occurred in 1 patient (0.4%) with an S-ICD and in 12 patients (4.8%) with TV-ICD. However, the S-ICD reduced perioperative, lead-related complications without significantly compromising the effectiveness of ICD shocks, but with more early postoperative pain and a trend for more inappropriate shocks [14].

## Patient Selection, Screening and Defibrillation Testing

Appropriate patient selection is central to S-ICD therapy. Because the device senses far-field surface-like signals, preimplant electrocardiographic screening is mandatory to minimise T-wave oversensing [15]. In one screening study, 8% failed the screening test, and patients with T-wave inversions in leads I, II, and aVF were 23 times more likely to fail. Inappropriate shocks have historically been a key limitation; compared with transvenous ICDs, S-ICDs have a lower rate of inappropriate shocks for supraventricular arrhythmias, but such shocks for T-wave oversensing and extracardiac myopotentials are more common [16]. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy patients are a particularly challenging group, in whom preimplantation screening has resulted in 14%–38% of patients being deemed inappropriate for S-ICD implantation [17]. Refinements to sensing algorithms, including high-pass filtering (SMART Pass), have reduced inappropriate shock rates [18].

Correct generator and lead positioning determines defibrillation success. The PRAETORIAN score, derived from chest radiographs, was developed because suboptimal positioning increases the defibrillation threshold and risk of conversion failure, providing a tool to evaluate implant position and predict defibrillation success [19]. Building on this, the PRAETORIAN-DFT trial investigated whether routine defibrillation testing could be safely omitted [20]; a subanalysis confirmed the score's predictive value for induced arrhythmia conversion [21], and design and screening considerations have been detailed elsewhere [22,23].

## Limitations and Future Directions

The principal limitation of the S-ICD is its inability to provide bradycardia pacing, antitachycardia pacing (ATP), or cardiac resynchronisation [24]. Postoperative pain is also more pronounced given the larger generator [25,26]. Two technological strategies address the pacing gap. The extravascular ICD (EV-ICD) uses a substernal lead; the EV-ICD has a single lead implanted substernally to enable pause-prevention pacing, antitachycardia pacing, and defibrillation energy similar to that of transvenous ICDs [27]. Long-term pivotal data support its durability [28]. The modular approach pairs the S-ICD with a wirelessly communicating leadless pacemaker; the MODULAR ATP trial demonstrated that this modular cardiac rhythm management system—a subcutaneous ICD in wireless communication with a leadless pacemaker capable of pace-terminating ventricular tachycardia—was feasible [29], with one-year outcomes confirming acceptable safety and performance [30].

## Conclusion

The S-ICD has matured into a validated alternative to the TV-ICD for patients without a pacing indication, offering comparable efficacy while avoiding intravascular lead complications. Careful screening and optimal implant positioning remain essential, and emerging extravascular and modular technologies promise to extend its applicability by restoring pacing capabilities.
